title: Autoregressive Language Model — 7 Learning Questions
subtitle: Topic: Next-Token Prediction and Sequential Language Generation · Subject: Transformers and LLM Architecture. Your seven original questions without redundant Layer prefixes, balanced A–D choices, unique visual diagrams, and beginner explanations with optional detail.
hero:
AUTOREGRESSIVE LANGUAGE MODEL · OVERVIEW

Predict. Append. Repeat.

Text grows one token at a time. Each new token becomes context for predicting the next.

questions.stem: What is an Autoregressive Language Model, and how does it generate human-like text by predicting the next token based on the tokens that have already appeared in a sequence?
options: An autoregressive model predicts every future token at once before looking at the prompt, so earlier text never influences its choices during generation.
An autoregressive language model predicts each next token based on the sequence of earlier tokens. It appends its choice and repeats, allowing previously generated text to shape later predictions.
An autoregressive model fills missing words using both left and right context, rather than continuing a sequence based only on what came earlier.
An autoregressive model labels the words in an existing sentence but never produces additional tokens, so its output cannot extend the input.
questions.explanation: Explanation: An autoregressive language model predicts each next token based on the sequence of earlier tokens. It appends its choice and repeats, allowing previously generated text to shape later predictions. Picture an AI composing a new instruction for a telescope operator. It sees the starting words, predicts the next token, then adds that token to the text. The next prediction uses the longer sequence. This is an autoregressive language model: each output depends on the preceding tokens. It does not choose the entire response simultaneously. Many GPT-style systems use this method.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: An autoregressive language model factorizes a sequence into conditional next-token probabilities. During inference it samples or selects a token based on the prefix, appends the token, and repeats until stopping.
questions.figure:
01 · THE BASIC IDEA

The model extends its own text, step by step

Each token gets added to the history used to predict the next.

questions.stem: Why is an Autoregressive Language Model described as "autoregressive," and how does predicting one token at a time differ from models that predict missing words or analyze an entire sentence simultaneously?
options: Autoregressive models require the complete future sentence to be visible before deciding the next word, which would defeat normal left-to-right generation.
Autoregressive models predict only missing words by reading both neighboring words, so their predictions cannot depend on earlier generated output.
Autoregressive models classify an entire passage once without using prior predictions, making their sequence generation independent from previously chosen tokens.

'Auto' refers to using previous elements of the same generated sequence. Unlike bidirectional masked-token modeling, a causal autoregressive generator cannot rely on future output tokens that do not yet exist.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Auto' refers to using previous elements of the same generated sequence. Unlike bidirectional masked-token modeling, a causal autoregressive generator cannot rely on future output tokens that do not yet exist. Think of a writer continuing a diary entry one line at a time. Each new line can depend on what was written earlier. The word autoregressive means the model uses earlier elements of the same sequence, including its own previous outputs, to predict the next. A masked-word model solves a different task: it may use context on both sides of a blank.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: Its output becomes part of its next input. Autoregressive models condition on preceding tokens, unlike bidirectional masked-language models that may use both left and right context to predict a missing token.
questions.figure:
02 · PREDICTION TASKS

Forward generation differs from filling a gap

An autoregressive model predicts what comes next; an infilling model can use surrounding words.

questions.stem: Imagine an Autoregressive Language Model receives the prompt "Once upon a time, there was a." How does it select the next token, add that token to the existing sequence, and continue generating a complete story through repeated predictions?
options: With a prompt such as 'Once upon a time', the model scores candidate next tokens, selects one, appends it and predicts again. The earlier choices influence all later conditionals.
The model copies the opening prompt unchanged and then attaches random completed paragraphs without checking whether they follow from the existing story.
The model predicts every sentence simultaneously, ignoring the words it generated earlier, so new sentences do not influence its later choices.
The model can only select a token that appeared in the initial prompt, making it unable to introduce characters or words from its vocabulary.
questions.explanation: Explanation: With a prompt such as 'Once upon a time', the model scores candidate next tokens, selects one, appends it and predicts again. The earlier choices influence all later conditionals. Start a story with “Once upon a time, there was a.” The model estimates which token might follow, perhaps “dragon,” “garden,” or “child.” A decoding rule chooses one. After appending the chosen token, the model calculates a new distribution based on the expanded story. It repeats until it reaches a stopping condition, such as an end token or length limit.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: Given the prompt, the model computes next-token logits and probabilities. Decoding selects a token, such as illustrative “ It,” appends it, then conditions the next prediction on the enlarged sequence. Probabilities shown are illustrative.

03 · STORY CONTINUATION

An example of selecting and appending the next token

questions.stem: How does an Autoregressive Language Model learn during training using teacher forcing, shifted input-target sequences, causal attention masks, and cross-entropy loss, and why can it calculate training losses for multiple token positions in parallel even though text generation happens sequentially?
options: Training feeds back sampled model tokens for each step and waits until the whole story finishes to calculate a single final loss value.
Training exposes future target tokens to every attention position, allowing the model to copy the answer rather than learn from preceding context.

Teacher forcing feeds correct earlier tokens, shifted labels supply next-token targets, and causal masks hide future targets. Cross-entropy trains many positions in parallel, unlike sequential output generation.
Training computes loss only for the last position of every sequence, ignoring earlier token predictions even when correct targets are available.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Teacher forcing feeds correct earlier tokens, shifted labels supply next-token targets, and causal masks hide future targets. Cross-entropy trains many positions in parallel, unlike sequential output generation. Imagine training a model on collections of short song titles. During training, the correct earlier tokens are already known. With teacher forcing, the model receives those true tokens, and shifted targets tell it what to predict next. A causal mask prevents positions from reading their future targets. Many positions can be evaluated in parallel, with cross-entropy providing learning signals.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: Teacher forcing supplies the true previous tokens, shifted labels give the next token at each position, and a causal mask blocks future input tokens. Cross-entropy losses are calculated in parallel during training even though generation remains sequential.
questions.figure:
04 · PARALLEL TRAINING

Teacher forcing aligns each input with its next-token target

Every position can learn at once because the causal mask hides future targets.

questions.stem: How does an Autoregressive Language Model mathematically represent the probability of a complete token sequence using the chain rule \(P(x_1,\ldots,x_T)=\prod\_{t=1}^{T}P(x_t\mid x_1,\ldots,x\_{t-1})\), and how are conditional probabilities converted into next-token predictions through logits, Softmax, and sampling?
options: The model adds independent token probabilities without considering earlier words, even though complete sequence likelihood depends on conditional context.
The model selects tokens directly from unnormalized scores, ignoring Softmax and any sampling choices that could influence the next generated token.
The chain rule factors sequence probability as a product of conditional token probabilities. Vocabulary logits become Softmax probabilities at each step; decoding chooses among candidate tokens.
The model calculates sentence probabilities by counting visible words, instead of estimating how likely each token follows its preceding context.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The chain rule factors sequence probability as a product of conditional token probabilities. Vocabulary logits become Softmax probabilities at each step; decoding chooses among candidate tokens. Suppose a model gives a sequence of three words probabilities of 0.5, 0.4, and 0.2, each conditioned on the preceding words. The chain rule multiplies them: 0.5 × 0.4 × 0.2 = 0.04 for that complete sequence. For each step, the model produces raw logits, and Softmax turns them into a distribution over candidate tokens. A decoding strategy chooses one.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: The chain rule gives P(x₁,…,x_T)=∏ P(x_t|x₁,…,x_{t−1}). The model predicts vocabulary logits, and Softmax converts them to conditional next-token probabilities. Sampling or greedy selection then chooses a token. For example, 0.50×0.20×0.60=0.06.
questions.figure:
05 · CHAIN RULE

Sequence probabilities multiply; Softmax produces next-token choices

Multiply conditional token probabilities for the whole sentence. Softmax converts logits into next-token probabilities.

questions.stem: How do Autoregressive Language Models such as GPT handle the differences between training and inference, including teacher forcing versus self-generated tokens, exposure bias, error accumulation, and the influence of decoding strategies such as temperature, Top-k, and Top-p sampling on generation quality?
options: Training and inference both receive correct earlier tokens from a labeled dataset, so a generated mistake cannot influence later predictions in either setting.

Training usually uses true previous tokens; inference uses its own earlier sampled tokens, allowing mistakes to compound (exposure bias). Temperature, top-k and top-p control selection without updating weights.
Temperature changes the model's learned context-window size, while Top-k and Top-p update weight matrices whenever the next token is sampled.
A wrong generated word has no influence on any following prediction, since each token is selected independently of the previously written text.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Training usually uses true previous tokens; inference uses its own earlier sampled tokens, allowing mistakes to compound (exposure bias). Temperature, top-k and top-p control selection without updating weights. Imagine a chatbot drafting museum exhibit labels. During training, it learns from correct word sequences; at inference, it must continue from words it actually generated. A poorly chosen token can change later predictions, a challenge related to exposure bias. Temperature changes the sharpness of its token distribution; Top-k or Top-p restrict sampling candidates.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: Teacher forcing conditions on ground-truth prefixes, whereas inference conditions on model-generated prefixes. This mismatch can cause exposure bias and error accumulation. Temperature rescales logits; top-k retains k candidates; top-p keeps the smallest candidate set passing a probability-mass threshold.
questions.figure:
06 · TRAINING VS INFERENCE

Generating with your own past can carry mistakes forward

Temperature changes randomness. Top-k and top-p filter candidate tokens.

questions.stem: What challenges arise when scaling Autoregressive Language Models for production use, including sequential decoding latency, KV-cache memory growth, long-context processing, hallucinations, and token-by-token computational costs, and how do techniques such as speculative decoding, continuous batching, prefix caching, and model distillation help improve inference efficiency while preserving output quality?
options: KV, prefix caches and continuous batching reuse work; speculative decoding verifies fast proposals and distillation reduces model cost. Measure tokens/second, time-to-first-token, memory and answer quality.
KV caching removes every memory requirement and makes every generated answer factually correct, regardless of context length or model limitations.
Speculative decoding accepts draft tokens without checking the target model, so it never needs to verify whether the proposed continuation is valid.
Long prompts require no additional attention work once old tokens have been cached, making generation time independent of the supplied context.
questions.explanation: Explanation: KV, prefix caches and continuous batching reuse work; speculative decoding verifies fast proposals and distillation reduces model cost. Measure tokens/second, time-to-first-token, memory and answer quality. Picture an online language tutor serving many students simultaneously. Generating text one token at a time can create latency. KV caching avoids recalculating earlier attention projections, continuous batching groups work from active requests, and prefix caching reuses common prompt computations. Speculative decoding verifies drafts proposed by a faster model. A distilled model can reduce compute.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: KV caches reuse prior attention states but grow with sequence length. Speculative decoding drafts several tokens and verifies them with a target model; proper acceptance can preserve the distribution. Continuous batching schedules active requests, prefix caching reuses common prompts, and distillation trains a smaller model with quality trade-offs. Hallucinations remain a separate reliability issue.

07 · AT SCALE

Memory and latency grow with longer generation

Caching and serving techniques can reduce repeated work, but output quality still needs checking.
